entries.title: EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig drone attack
entries.summary: The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the attempted attack had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." She said the EU was summoning a Russian envoy, with France announcing a similar step.
entries.content:
Germany

EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig drone attack

September 2, 2026

The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the attempted attack had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." She said the EU was summoning a Russian envoy, with France announcing a similar step.

The European Unions's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday that she summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels over the alleged attempted hybrid attack involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month. 

Germany's foreign and interior ministers said in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the government in Berlin had concluded that Russia was responsible for the failed attack, reinforcing suspicions that arose as soon as the news broke in August. 

Kallas says incident has 'all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism'

"We are discussing the Leipzig attacks, and also it is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism," Kallas said ahead of an informal gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.

"The question is, what do we do about this? We have already summoned the Russian ambassador," she said.

The former Estonian prime minister also said that the EU was continuing its work on its next package of some 1,600 sanctions listings related to Russia's war in Ukraine and said "maybe there is more to be added."

France takes similar step, summoning charge d'affaires

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also told reporters in Dublin that Paris was summoning a Russian ambassador in response. 

"I have summoned the Russian charge d'affaires in Paris to protest, Barrot said, adding that sanctions should be taken at a European level, notably against Russia's so-called shadow fleet of ships.

Non-EU foreign ministers from Ukraine, the UK, Canada, Norway, Iceland and Switzerland also traveled to Ireland to attend Wednesday's informal talks.

Germany's Wadephul says 'pressure on Russia is being stepped up'

German Foreign Minsiter Johann Wadephul told reporters that the EU would continue to work on additional sanctions "in the coming weeks." 

"Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Urkaine also remains at a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at this time," he said.

The Christian Democrat politician said that Russia had chosen to escalate, and "must now live with these consequences."

He also defended Tuesday's announcement in Berlin, calling the government's response a "necessary and proportionate" one based on a "well-founded opinion and verdict."

What did Germany say about its investigations?

Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the federal government in Berlin held Russia responsible for the failed attack. 

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," Dobrindt said on Tuesday, without going into specifics.

Wadephul said that the "means used — drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine." 

Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, have rejected the allegations and accused Germany of fabricating its version of events.

Leipzig/Halle Airport is a key freight hub. Ukrainian airline and aircraft manufacturer Antonov uses the airport as a base of operations, frequently transiting material to Ukraine via the the eastern German city.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: What really helps Europe deal with drought
entries.summary: Fix leaks, or ban pools? As European countries prepare for hotter, drier years to come, here's what the data says about how to really save water
entries.content:
September 2, 2026

Fix leaks, or ban pools? As European countries prepare for hotter, drier years to come, here's what the data says about how to really save water

Europe is in drought. As the burning of fossil fuels pushes up temperatures that are making summers hotter and drier, the continent's soils, lakes and rivers are struggling to recover. Southern and Western European countries are particularly affected. But they're not the only ones.

"We've seen drought risks expanding northward during the last decade", says Gisela Elsner, Climate and Sustainability Policy Officer at the German Konrad Adenauer Foundation, who has followed EU water management efforts for years.

"Central and Western Europe, but also southeastern European countries, are increasingly vulnerable due to climate change."

For the month of August this year, satellite data shows areas as far north as Denmark and Sweden experiencing extremely dry conditions more often seen in regions such as the Sub-Saharan Sahel.

The impact is palpable. Some of the continent's longest rivers like the Rhine or the Danube have reached historic lows, disrupting inland shipping routes. Farmers from Germany to Ukraine are reporting below-average harvests, and areas from the United Kingdom to Switzerland to Germany have announced restrictions on household water use.

To make matters worse, this year's El Niño event — a climate cycle that weakens trade winds and warms tropical Pacific surface temperatures — is set to be one of the strongest on record. Experts predict that 2027 will be even hotter and drier as a result.

Europe will have to adapt to this reality, says Gisela Elsner. "It is not yet a matter of not having water in our taps anymore. But we need to prioritize and use our water resources efficiently."

So, how can countries across the continent set about doing this? DW analyzed water usage in European nations and reviewed the evidence to find out which measures have the most impact.

Which European countries use the most water?

Private households in Europe account for a relatively small share of water usage. Depending on the country, they consume a daily per capita average of between 50 and 300 liters, which equates to less than 20% of all use.

Two thirds of water withdrawn continent-wide is for agriculture — mostly for irrigation — as well as electricity cooling for nuclear and fossil fuel power plants.

In already drought-prone countries like Greece, Turkey and Spain, agriculture accounts for most of the near 2000 liters of water withdrawn per person each day.

Electricity cooling is the biggest factor in Eastern European countries like Bulgaria or Hungary, but also in the Netherlands or Estonia, which use between 1000 and 2000 liters per capita daily in total.

Where Europe can save the most water

"There is no single solution that is sufficient to solve this challenge," says Gisela Elsner. "It has to be a combined bundle of measures."

And they exist. A recent report published by the European Environmental Agency (EEA) found that EU countries could save between 10 and 40% of water annually by implementing targeted strategies.

For states in Western and Eastern Europe, shifting to clean energy would make a big difference. While nuclear, and planet-heating oil, gas and coal need huge amounts of water for cooling, wind and solar do not.

Electricity cooling: renewables to the rescue

So besides becoming the cheapest forms of energy, the renewables that are increasingly replacing fossil fuels are also helping countries to save water. Over the past two decades, Europe has reduced its water usage by around a quarter — mostly because of more efficient electrical cooling.

Even with nuclear plants still requiring water in countries like France, Spain or Sweden, the potential savings are massive. The EEA estimates that EU countries could make significant further savings of between 45 and 95% — equal to hundreds of liters per person each day — by expanding renewables and improving cooling systems.

Better irrigation can help in agriculture

In Southern Europe, agriculture is the big-ticket item. The EEA report recommends, for instance, replacing open water transport channels with closed pipes to avoid evaporation during heatwaves, switching from surface irrigation to sprinklers or drip irrigation, and opting for less water-intensive crops whereever possible.

Public water supply: leaky pipes lose lots of water

In EU countries, around one in four liters of drinkable water from the public supply is lost to leaky pipes and evaporation before it ever reaches its destination — according to estimates by the European association of water providers EurEau.

In Romania and Italy, the share is more than 40%. According to the EEA report, avoiding these losses would account for most of the potential savings in the EU's public water supply.

Once drinking water reaches households and businesses, individual behavior has an impact as well. The EEA report lists extensive recommendations for savings in daily life, from low-flow toilets and efficient washing machines and dishwashers, to harvesting rainwater. Yet even if every citizen in Europe did all they could, it would only reduce the daily per person household water use by between 10 and 40%.

Citizens could also contribute through more responsible consumer decisions, such as considering the water footprint of the products they buy or support, says Alexander Psomas, water resources expert at the Greek consultancy Brilliant Solutions, who co-authored the EEA report.

"Citizens can also push our governments to be more accountable on their energy policy and the impact it has on water."

What Europe can learn

Drought and heat waves are not just a European problem. Many parts in the world are even more severely affected by the climate crisis. And data from the United Nations shows regions in Northern Africa, the Middle East and Asia have been dealing with much higher levels of water stress for a long time.

This also means that Europe can collaborate with, and learn from, the rest of the world on how to adapt to water scarcity. "The UN World Food Program and the FAO are all working on similar questions in the Global South," said Giriraj Armanath, Research Group Leader at the International Water Management Institute.

Gisela Elsner recounts, for instance, chip manufacturers in the German state of Saxony recently looking to expertise from Singapore on how to reuse wastewater to cool their factories.

"We can definitely learn from those countries which already have all the knowledge and the technologies that can be used in our context as well," she said.

Public and politics are paying more attention to water use

Both Gisela Elsner and Alexander Psomas say they have noticed both politics and the public becoming more aware in recent years.

"The water scarcity and droughts topic did not have a relevant EU working group until 2022", Psomas told DW. "Today, it's one of the working groups with the highest participation. There is a growing interest and concern on this issue."

What he would like to see more of, he says, is public debates about water strategies, especially during election periods.

"If a country runs low on water, it affects everyone," he says. "I would like to see politicians discuss what kind of solutions they're offering for making their countries more water resilient in 10, 20 years from now."

Edited by Tamsin Walker and Gianna Grün



All data and code behind this analysis can be found in this Github repository. More data-driven stories by DW can be found here.

entries.title: Charlie Kirk murder suspect to face potential death penalty
entries.summary: Tyler R., accused of fatally shooting Charlie Kirk, will stand trial on aggravated murder charges after a Utah judge ruled prosecutors had enough evidence to seek the death penalty.
entries.content:
September 2, 2026

Tyler R., accused of fatally shooting Charlie Kirk, will stand trial on aggravated murder charges after a Utah judge ruled prosecutors had enough evidence to seek the death penalty.

The murder case against Tyler R., the man accused of fatally shooting conservative activist Charlie Kirk last September, is headed to trial, and he could face the death penalty if convicted, under a new ruling. 

Utah District Judge Tony Graf ruled late on Tuesday that prosecutors had presented sufficient evidence to proceed, ordering that the defendant be set for trial.

The 23-year-old suspect pleaded not guilty to all seven charges, including aggravated murder, following the ruling. A hearing to schedule the trial date is set for October 23.

What did the prosecutors say?

Prosecutors say Tyler R. fired a single shot from a rooftop more than 400 feet (~122 meters) away, striking 31-year-old Kirk in the neck as he addressed a crowd of more than 3,000 people at Utah Valley University. 

A strong supporter of President Donald Trump, Kirk has been credited with motivating young voters to turn out for him in the 2024 US presidential election.

Utah County prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court the defendant "lay down in a prone position, and he would have seen this mass of people, of 3,000-plus people there for the event, took aim, put his crosshairs on Charlie Kirk and fired."

McBride argued the shooting "created a great risk of death that anyone would know about."

Prosecutors also pointed to the rifle's additional unfired rounds as evidence that the suspect "came prepared to shoot again," and presented DNA evidence they say ties him to the weapon and to a tool allegedly used to engrave one of the cartridges with the words "Hey Fascist! CATCH!"

What did the defense say?

The defendant's attorneys have argued the case does not meet Utah's legal threshold for aggravated murder, which requires showing that others faced a high probability, not just a possibility, of harm.

Defense attorney Staci Visser told the court, "There is one act. There is one shot. There is one bullet. There is one victim," adding that there was "zero evidence that there was any action taken towards other people."

The defense also challenged the reliability of the prosecution's DNA testing.

Court hears argument for political motive

Prosecutors say the defendant targeted Kirk over his political views, citing a text message in which he allegedly wrote to his roommate, "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out." 

A handwritten note he reportedly wrote the roommate, who he was romantically involved with, read: "I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it."

However, defense attorney Richard Novak countered that Kirk had spoken "hatefully" about LGBTQ people and that the wording of the message didn't necessarily indicate a political motive.

Kirk family welcomes 'important step' for justice

Kirk's parents and widow, Erika Kirk, who now leads his organization Turning Point USA, attended the hearing. In a statement, the Kirk family said the ruling "marks an important step in our family's pursuit of justice for him."

"Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father," read the statement posted by Erika Kirk on social media.

Legal analyst Seth Zuckerman told Reuters he expects the case to go to trial rather than end in a plea deal, saying prosecutors "may not be willing to take the death penalty off the table, and that would probably require a trial."

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Women's football: Anyomi, London City and the German exodus
entries.summary: Nicole Anyomi has joined Alexia Putellas and other star names in signing for the ambitious English club London City Lionesses. The Germany winger told DW England is a better place to develop her game than back home.
entries.content:
Germany

Women's football: Anyomi, London City and the German exodus

September 2, 2026

Nicole Anyomi has joined Alexia Putellas and other star names in signing for the ambitious English club London City Lionesses. The Germany winger told DW England is a better place to develop her game than back home.

The London City Lionesses have existed for less than a decade, have played in England's top flight for just one season and can't play in the Champions League. Yet, having broken the women's transfer record last year, the Lionesses have signed some of the game's biggest stars for the coming season as their ambition becomes ever more apparent.

As well as two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas and her Spanish teammate Mapi Leon, England's Euro 2022 winning goalkeeper Mary Earps and French star Kadidiatou Diani, Germany winger Nicole Anyomi is among the new arrivals.

Anyomi left Eintracht Frankfurt, where she'd scored 50 goals in 101 Bundesliga games over five years, for what she considers a greater challenge in England.

The 'perfect step'

"The next step was to go to the league to compete every single weekend and this is what I see here in this league," she told DW.

"I have some friends who already played in the WSL (Women's Super League) and they told me about the league so I think this will be the perfect step for me."

Anyomi is one of several players to leave Germany's Women's Bundesliga for England this summer. Among them are Anyomi's international teammates Vivien Endemann (Wolfsburg to Liverpool), Selina Cerci (Hoffenheim to Arsenal), Carlotta Wamser (Bayer Leverkusen to Manchester City) and England's Georgia Stanway (Bayern Munich to Arsenal).

Anyomi pointed to the increasing gap in infrastructure, finances and coaching as the primary reasons for the exodus.

"In Germany you have two, three teams who are competing at the top but here in England there are five, six, seven, eight teams.

"Also, the facilities and the staff members. We have 30-plus staff members here whereas in Frankfurt we had like seven or eight. You can learn from each person and there is something new to learn every day. I think that's how you develop as a player faster."

Germany falling further behind?

With England's national team having won the last two Euros, a competition once dominated by Germany, and no German side having won the Champions League since 2015, there is a concern that Germany rested on its laurels for too long.

In an effort to address this issue, last December, the Frauen-Bundesliga FBL e.V. (Women's Bundesliga Association) was formed. Similar to the DFL, which operates the men's Bundesliga, the FBL is designed to improve the league's marketing and increase revenue. It is to take over operation of the league next July 1. 

"They have to bring something, not new, but something different into the league so maybe the players would stay," Anyomi said.

"I think it's an investment thing, but I think now they are building something new, to do different things. I'm going to see this season of course and watch the Bundesliga. I hope they are going to invest more, do more for the league so players also from abroad can come to Germany."

Her new club are the foremost example of the changing face of women's football. London City did not exist until 2019 when, effectively, they took over the license of another team, Milwall. Their progress has recently been accelerated by Michelle Kang.

The Korean-American businesswoman is a serial investor in women's football and added London City to an ownership portfolio that includes serial Champions League winners OL Lyonnes and US side Washington Spirit in December 2023. Kang's deep pockets and ambition mean London City are on track to compete at the top end of the WSL within the next few years.

Kang ownership presents possibility and prohibition

But her ownership of OL Lyonnes prohibits London City from playing in the Champions League. UEFA, who organize the tournament, have enshrined laws that mean clubs that are in multi-ownership structures cannot both be in the same competition in the same season. Last season, in the men's game, this led to English side Crystal Palace being demoted from the Europa League to the Europa Conference league.

"Why would we want to preserve the sporting integrity of men's football, but not of women's football? It's out of the question," said UEFA's head of women's football and former Germany international, Nadine Kessler earlier this year.

"In any sport you want to preserve sporting integrity, that's the most important thing."

Anyomi, who must recover from a hamstring injury before she can make her debut, said she trusts the club, who have so far "done everything they promised" to find a solution.

But the lack of continental football means fewer chances to make her mark alongside the other new arrivals. Given that the World Cup in Brazil is at the end of the coming season, the move could be seen by some as a risk.

"I did think about that because I know I have to play at the club level, otherwise I won't be selected," she said. "I wanted to go abroad two years ago and I didn't in the end, so I decided to go this summer. I had the feeling this is the right step."

Whether it's to London City, or to the WSL more broadly, she's not the only Bundesliga player to feel that way.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Cargo ship with 10 crew sinks off Turkey coast — authorities
entries.summary: Coast guard vessels and a helicopter are searching for 10 missing crew members off the coast of Istanbul. Authorities say they lost contact after the bulk carrier crashed into a chemical tanker off the coast of Istanbul.
entries.content:
Turkey

Cargo ship with 10 crew sinks off Turkey coast — authorities

September 2, 2026

Coast guard vessels and a helicopter are searching for 10 missing crew members off the coast of Istanbul. Authorities say they lost contact after the bulk carrier crashed into a chemical tanker off the coast of Istanbul.

Turkish authorities are searching for 10 people aboard a cargo ship that sank after a collision with another vessel in the Marmara Sea near Istanbul early Wednesday.

"We believe, and have more or less confirmed, that the Tugberk Imamoglu has sunk," Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu told reporters in Istanbul.

Uraloglu said all 10 crew members aboard the vessel were Turkish nationals and that attempts to reach them by mobile phone had been unsuccessful.

"We can say that the sinking occurred rapidly in 11 minutes. No one has been found alive," he added.

The bulk carrier Tugberk Imamoglu and the chemical tanker Alsu collided at around 3 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) off the city's western Silivri district, the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement.

Two helicopters and 12 search and rescue vessels are scouring the area.

The Transport Ministry's maritime directorate said that life-saving equipment, including a lifeboat belonging to the Tugberk Imamoglu, had been found floating on the surface.

"Unfortunately, the crew members were not inside," it added.

What else do we know about the missing ship?

The 90-meter (295-foot) Turkish-flagged bulk carrier was en route to the Black Sea ​port ‌of Eregli from Iskenderun when the collision happened.

According to the maritime directorate, it was carrying 4,200 tons of rolled steel.

Authorities believe it sank in waters around 900 meters deep.

The 91-meter Turkish-flagged Alsu, was sailing from Kocaeli, east of Istanbul, to the Aegean port of Aliaga. It was empty at the time of the collision and did not appear to have suffered any damage, the governor's office said.

The Sea of Marmara forms part of one of the world's busiest shipping corridors, linking the Mediterranean to the Black Sea via the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Germany news: Terror probe opened in power station attack
entries.summary: Police are investigating after homemade projectiles were used to damage power lines in eastern Germany. This comes amid suspicion of sabotage another power station in the west of the country. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published September 2, 2026last updated September 2, 2026

Police are investigating after homemade projectiles were used to damage power lines in eastern Germany. This comes amid suspicion of sabotage another power station in the west of the country. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Minor injuries reported after object explodes near Augsburg train station
  • Police are investigating 'criminal act' at power station near Cologne, North-Rhine Westphalia
  • Authorities also opened a terror probe over Tuesday's sabotage of a power station in Brandenburg
  • Germany is weighing further action against Russia after announcing it was behind the drone incident at Leipzig airport

Read below for a roundup of news and analysis from and concerning Germany on Tuesday, September 1.

Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here  to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google. 

Skip next section Police open terrorism investigation after Brandenburg grid sabotage

Police open terrorism investigation after Brandenburg grid sabotage

Police in the eastern German state of Brandenburg on Wednesday said they were investigating the possible formation of a terrorist organization in connection with an attack on a power plant and substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg.

According to officials, on Tuesday morning, a projectile managed to carry a cable into the extra-high-voltage power line at a substation near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant, creating a conductive connection to the ground that caused a brief outage.

On Wednesday, Brandenburg's state Interior Minister Jan Redmann said "we were damn lucky" that only one of more than a dozen "rocket-like objects equipped with a propellant charge" reached its target.

He added the suspects had positioned the projectiles directly beneath the power lines near the Turnow-Preilack substation on the border with the state of Saxony.

The search for suspects continues, and an investigation is looking into all possibilities.

Brandenburg police said their investigation also includes disruption of public services, the causing of an explosion and the destruction of important equipment.

"At this point, we must assume that the perpetrators had been on the scene for several days beforehand and had installed the necessary equipment," Redmann said.

The construction and installation of the devices required a considerable amount of "technical expertise," he added.

Skip next section ICE train stops after door opened at 200 km/h

ICE train stops after door opened at 200 km/h

A German high-speed Intercity Express (ICE) train was forced to stop near the entrance of a tunnel on Tuesday after a door mysteriously opened during the ride, police said Wednesday.

The train had been moving at around 200 km/h (125 mph) and the conductor immediately applied the emergency brakes.

There were 238 passengers on board the train, which was heading from Munich to Dortmund. No injuries were reported after police searched the tracks and ruled out the possibility someone could have fallen through the door.

The passengers were able to get off the train in the town of Lohr am Main.

Germany's Federal Police interviewed the passengers there and took down personal information. The officers also checked to see if any luggage had fallen off the train. The rail line was reopened around 2:30 a.m.

According to a railway spokeswoman, there was no technical malfunction with the train.

German rail operator Deutsche Bahn declined to comment on whether someone on board the train might have opened the door intentionally.

"Doors on the ICE don't just open while the train is moving," according to a brief statement given to Germany's DPA news agency.

"The specific cause is being investigated by the authorities," it added.

Further details will not be available until the investigation is complete.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany terminates lease for 'Russian House' in Berlin

IN DEPTH: Germany terminates lease for 'Russian House' in Berlin

After Germany on Tuesday said Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at an airport in Leipzig, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that the contract for the cultural center "Russian House" would be cancelled.

The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it has long been the subject of fierce disagreements and a bone of contention in Berlin.

Skip next section Augsburg station reopens after police give all clear

Augsburg station reopens after police give all clear

Augsburg train station reopened after police sealed off the area while investigating an early morning blast that left two passers-by aged 17 and 18 with minor acoustic trauma.

According to the Bild tabloid, police said a hand grenade exploded outside a jewelry shop next to the station, causing minor damage to the facade. Police have not immediately confirmed the report of a grenade.

Police had completely shut down the station after a bomb sniffing dog uncovered a second "suspicious object," which turned out to be fragments of the grenade, Bild reported.

There was no further information available on suspects or a motive.

Skip next section German FM says new EU Russia sanctions coming soon

German FM says new EU Russia sanctions coming soon

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Wednesday said that the European Union is working on imposing more sanctions on Russian individuals in the coming weeks, a day after Germany said Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport on August 4. 

"Russia has escalated and must live with the consequences," Wadephul said at a gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.

"Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Ukraine also remains at ​a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at ⁠this ​time," he said, without sharing further details on what the new measures would entail, other than they would target "a large number" of individuals.

The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said that the Leipzig incident had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." adding that the EU was working on sanctions targeting 1,600 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military industry.

Officials had discovered a drone between Ukrainian cargo aircraft fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism, triggering speculation over who could have been responsible. 

On Tuesday, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that although the devices required "a high degree of technical expertise," the plan appears to have been carried out by "low-level" agents.

The ministers said the Russian consulate general in Bonn would be closed, along with the termination of the lease for the Russian House, a Russian cultural institution in the heart of Berlin.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected Germany's accusations and said the punitive measures are a "serious mistake."

Skip next section WATCH: Germany blames Russia for attempted Leipzig drone attack

WATCH: Germany blames Russia for attempted Leipzig drone attack

During a press conference on Tuesday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul disclosed intelligence findings about the incident in which an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig Airport last month.

Skip next section Augsburg station closed due to 'suspicious object'

Augsburg station closed due to 'suspicious object'

Police in Augsburg have said the city's main train station is now fully shut down as of 8:30 a.m. with rail service suspended, due to a "suspicious object," without sharing further details.

Earlier, one track had been operating as police investigated a blast from an unknown object earlier Wednesday morning.

Skip next section Unidentified object explodes near Augsburg train station, injuring 2

Unidentified object explodes near Augsburg train station, injuring 2

An unidentified object exploded near a train station in the southern German city of Augsburg early Wednesday morning, with two people sustaining minor injuries due to acoustic trauma, police said.

Window panes were also reportedly damaged by the explosion, which occurred in a building passageway.

No information is yet available regarding the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Parts of the station were closed off as police continued investigating the scene. The State Criminal Police Office (LKA) is on the scene with an explosive-disposal robot, the Augsburger Allgemeine newspaper reported.

Police first responded to the incident at around 5 a.m. local time.

Augsburg is ⁠a ​regional ​transport hub ​around 55 ‌kilometers (35 miles) west ​of ⁠Munich.

Skip next section Police label power station disruption in Bergheim a 'deliberate act'

Police label power station disruption in Bergheim a 'deliberate act'

Police are investigating a disruption at a power station in the town of Bergheim in western Germany, near Cologne. 

On Tuesday evening, several power lines failed following a short circuit at the power station.

"Based on the current status of the investigation, we do not believe this was caused by a technical malfunction, but rather by a deliberate act, a criminal offense," a police spokesperson said on Wednesday morning.

The spokesperson did not initially provide any details regarding the damage or the actions of the alleged perpetrators.

Police said the incident on Tuesday evening did not cause a power outage to the surrounding area.

The incident comes as tensions are high after unknown individuals attempted to cause short circuits in extra-high-voltage power lines near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday morning.

Police found explosive devices near the plant are investigating the incident as an act of sabotage.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten morgen from DW's newsroom in Bonn.

This morning we are looking at reports of a blast at a train station in the southern city of Augsburg. Police said two people were lightly injured and the cause is still unclear.

And near Cologne, police said they suspect a disruption at a power station last night was the result of a criminal act. An investigation is ongoing.

entries.title: Tunisia's human rights defenders decry civil society crackdown
entries.summary: Five years into the authoritarian rule of Tunisian President Kais Saied, Human Rights Watch and other activists warn that Tunisia's once vibrant civil society is in danger of being completely stifled.
entries.content:
Tunisia

Tunisia's rights defenders decry civil society crackdown

September 2, 2026

Five years into the authoritarian rule of Tunisian President Kais Saied, Human Rights Watch and other activists warn that Tunisia's once vibrant civil society is in danger of being completely stifled.

"Most civil society organizations are in a state of shock today," Messaoud Romdhani, a Tunisian human rights activist told DW. "Those who criticize the authorities or situation in Tunisia face widespread repression," he explained, adding that "most have been accused of money laundering, which leads to the suspension of their activities."

Another Tunisian activist, who spoke with DW on condition of anonymity, also said that increasingly people were thinking twice before speaking in public or even choosing to work on sensitive issues.

"What worries me most is the chilling effect: When organizations face suspension and activists face prosecution or detention, the uncertainty itself becomes a form of pressure," he said.

 Human Rights Watch has also raised the alarm. In its latest report, published Wednesday morning, the international rights watchdog concludes that Saied is attempting to shutter Tunisia's civil society entirely. 

"It is clear that the authorities are abusing every tool at their disposal to close the space for civil society in Tunisia," the report reads. The watchdog also points out that civil society groups in Tunisia have played a key role in holding power to account, delivering essential services and advocating for people's human rights.

"The government has used abusive, arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and suspension of organizations in an attempt to stifle these voices," Bassam Khawaja, a deputy director in the Middle East and North Africa Division at Human Rights Watch and editor of the report, told DW.

He added that it was clear the idea was to shut down all opposition and independent voices in the country. "This amounts to a total crackdown on civil society in Tunisia," he said. 

Saied was elected president democratically in 2019. But in July 2021, he dissolved parliament and launched a power grab. Since then, he has dismantled most democratic bodies, repressed political dissent and arrested opposition figures.

For Anthony Dworkin, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations who focuses on human rights and democracy, Saied's goals remain unchanged. "They have been the same for the last five years, namely to consolidate power and remove potential checks on and critics of his rule," he told DW.

Saied has rejected accusations that he is an authoritarian ruler and argued that his measures are necessary to tackle corruption and uphold democracy. He has accused critics of receiving foreign funding to stir unrest and undermine Tunisia's national interests. DW reached out to the Tunisian presidency for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.

Growing discontent prompts calls for Saied's resignation

Despite the widespread crackdown on dissent, some people still dare criticize the government. On July 25, the fifth anniversary of the president's power grab, thousands took to the streets of the capital, Tunis, to protest worsening living conditions, democratic backsliding and the government's handling of basic services.

The demonstrations came amid widespread water and electricity outages, which Saied has described as "premeditated acts aimed at inflaming the situation by all means and spreading lies and rumors to sow confusion."

In late August, protesters once again called on the president to step down by chanting "The people want the fall of the regime," a popular slogan from the 2010-2011 Arab Spring uprising.

The demonstration was initiated by Nafas, a new citizen-led umbrella initiative that was launched in May. Mohamed Hawel, a university teacher and member of the Nafas collective, told the news agency AP that Nafas was created to unite people around basic necessities, including water, electricity and food.

Growing gap between older, younger Tunisians

Despite some unity at these protests, according to an Arab Barometersurvey there is an emerging generational divide in Tunisia. A report published in July on the basis of a survey conducted in the fall of 2025 found that older and less educated people had vastly different views on the country's economic and political conditions from younger, better educated people.

The survey showed that the older generation saw the current political and economic situation in the most positive light since the Arab Spring and had more trust in the government than over the past decade.

In comparison, younger Tunisians were more pessimistic about the country's economic and political development. They also remained more skeptical of state institutions while maintaining a high trust in civil society organizations: 49% of people between the ages of 18-39 expressed trust in these, compared with only 32% of those aged 40 and older.

"What really stands out in Tunisia is that the recent decline in trust in civil society is almost entirely a story about older Tunisians. Two years prior, there was almost no generational gap between citizens," Michael Robbins, the director of Arab Barometer, told DW. "Since then, trust in civil society among Tunisians 40 and older has fallen quite sharply, while it has not changed meaningfully among those who are aged 18-39."

Tunisia has a population of approximately 12 million people. People aged 18–39 account for roughly 30% of the population, while those aged 40 and older account for approximately 43%.

"I think the notion of a divided society is overstated," said Dworkin. "Moreover, the recent demonstrations are not large enough to pose a serious threat to Kais Saied," he added, while admitting that Saied had lost considerable public support over his failure to improve the country's economy. "But there are no attractive political alternatives and people are also tired of political upheaval."

In his view, many Tunisians are just trying to get by with daily life, while many others are looking to emigrate.

DW's Tarek Guizani in Tunis contributed to this report.

entries.title: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty to collusion
entries.summary: The prominent activist pleaded guilty to colluding with foreign entities. He faces a lengthy prison sentence.
entries.content:
Hong Kong

Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty to collusion

September 2, 2026

The prominent activist pleaded guilty to colluding with foreign entities. He faces a lengthy prison sentence.

Pro-democracy Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong on Wednesday pleaded guilty to a charge of colluding with foreign entities.

Wong, who is already serving a nearly five-year prison sentence for subversion, was due to be released next year and could face up to life in prison.

What was Wong accused of?

Wong was accused of conspiring with fellow activist Nathan Law and others to ask foreign countries, or institutions, organizations, or individuals to impose sanctions or engage in other hostile actions against Hong Kong or China between July and November, 2020.

Wong sat in the courtroom dock as the charges were read out, before confirming his guilty plea, AFP journalists reported from inside the court.

He smiled and nodded after someone in the public gallery shouted "hang in there!"

Among those attending proceedings were several Western diplomats.

Who is Joshua Wong?

Wong first became widely known in Hong Kong as a teenager in 2012 when he led protests against national education being introduced in the city's schools.

In 2014, he rose to fame as one of the student leaders in the city's Occupy Movement, during which demonstrators occupied streets for 79 days while calling for direct elections for Hong Kong's leader.

However, Wong's efforts to garner overseas support for protests angered Beijing, which labelled him an advocate of Hong Kong independence who had "begged for interference" from foreign forces.

The political party he co-founded, Demosisto, was disbanded after the security law was enacted on June 30, 2020.

The 29-year-old was among dozens of activists arrested in 2021 for taking part in an unofficial poll to select candidates for a 2020 legislative council election.

His protest efforts have effectively been outlawed by Beijing's sweeping national security law.

Critics say Wong’s case illustrates the lengths to which authorities are willing to go to silence prominent dissidents.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Iran war: US, Tehran trade fire in new flare-up
entries.summary: Explosions have been reported around the Strait of Hormuz, including at an airport in southern Iran. US President Donald Trump said the strikes were a response to Iranian attempts to mine the strait. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran war: US, Tehran trade fire in new flare-up

Published September 1, 2026last updated September 2, 2026

Explosions have been reported around the Strait of Hormuz, including at an airport in southern Iran. US President Donald Trump said the strikes were a response to Iranian attempts to mine the strait. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Below is a roundup of the top headlines on the Iran war and other developments in the Middle East region on Tuesday, September 1, 2026.

  • US military says it has launched strikes on Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)
  • US President Trump described the strikes as 'large and powerful'
  • Iran said the US would 'regret' the latest attacks
  • Jordanian military says it intercepted Iranian missiles in Jordanian airspace
  • Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq's Kurdistan region also targeted by Iranian attacks

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section USS Abraham Lincoln arrives in Thailand after Middle East deployment

USS Abraham Lincoln arrives in Thailand after Middle East deployment

The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier docked at the port of Laem Chabang in eastern Thailand on Wednesday after a lengthy deployment in the Middle East.

The massive nuclear-powered vessel, carrying some 5,000 American service members, has spent 286 days at sea and was involved in the US naval blockade of Iranian ports as well as combat operations in the Middle East war.

The length of the deployment had raised concerns amid reports about deteriorating mental health among the crew and shortages of supplies on board.

During the five days in port, many service members are expected to visit the nearby beach resort town of Pattaya. While the stop is likely to boost local businesses, it's also drawn some scrutiny given Pattaya's reputation as a hub for sex tourism.

US service members have reportedly been barred from visiting the most notorious of the city's streets, as well as cannabis shops, and will be unable to engage in water sports such as jet-skiing.

"Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our sailors and Marines to rest and recharge," Rear Admiral Robert Loughran, commander of the US Carrier Strike Group 3, said in a statement.

Skip next section Two tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz — IRCG

Two tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz — IRCG

Two oil tankers have caught fire after hitting sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said in a statement.

The IRGCsaid the tankers were attempting "at the urging of the US military to transit via an illegal route" in the strait before "striking mines and exploding."

It said the vessels had been forced to disembark their crews. The information has not been independently verified.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's national shipping company Bahri said two sailors were killed in an attack on one of its vessels in the strait on Monday.

It said its oil tanker Sidr was "involved in a security incident while transiting the Strait of Hormuz" on the evening of August 31. Two Filipino crew were killed in the attack, it added.

The Strait of Hormuz was a key waterway for the transport of oil and gas before the Middle East war broke out in February. Iranian attacks on ships have largely brought traffic there to a halt, although some tankers have moved through the strait in recent weeks.

Skip next section Pakistan says it remains engaged with Iran, US to end conflict

Pakistan says it remains engaged with Iran, US to end conflict

Pakistan said it remains engaged with the US and Iran ‌on talks to end their conflict and was optimistic that the countries "will return to ‌the table for dialogue," Foreign Ministry ‌spokesperson Tahir Andrabi ‌told the media during his weekly briefing on Wednesday.

 

Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), which was held from August 31 to September 1 in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.

 

The spokesperson added that Pakistan's Chief of Defense Forces Asim Munir's visit to Tehran last week was also part of the country's push to put an end to the US-Iran conflict. 

 

He said the visit "generated momentum" ‌on a range of issues, including the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Skip next section Iran reports 11 civilian deaths in US strikes

Iran reports 11 civilian deaths in US strikes

Separate US attacks in southwestern Iran have killed 11 people and injured dozens more, Iranian state media reported on Wednesday.

In Hormozgan province, which straddles the Strait of Hormuz, four people, including a child, were killed after shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a residential home in the costal city of Kuhestak where a wedding was taking place, according to the Iranian Red Crescent. More than 50 people were reported injured.

AFP news agency reported a video shared by an Iranian government account showed extensive debris and damage at what it said was the site of the wedding in Sirik country.

"This cruelty cannot be separated from the chain of atrocities that preceded ​it," Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in a statement, pointing to previous attacks including a strike on a girls' school in Minab in February that killed 160 people.

Elsewhere, officials in Khuzestan province further to the north said US missile attacks on three locations in the province killed seven people and injured eight.

US officials did not directly address reports of the strike on a wedding, but US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson Tim Hawkins said "the US military never targets civilians."

Skip next section WATCH: Fighting Iran war, can US military sustain a long conflict?

WATCH: Fighting Iran war, can US military sustain a long conflict?

Six months into the Iran war, US military leaders are warning of stretched forces and depleted weapons stockpiles. Does the US have the resources to keep fighting?

Skip next section Iran's Revolutionary Guards say US bases targeted in Iraq's Kurdistan region

Iran's Revolutionary Guards say US bases targeted in Iraq's Kurdistan region

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had launched strikes on US bases with drones and missiles in Erbil, Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, according to state media.

State-run IRNA reported that the IRGC said they had "carried out a coordinated missile and drone attack on US bases in Erbil" and had destroyed a maintenance facility, warehouses and the "guidance system of a US surveillance aerostat."

The claims cannot be independently verified. The US military has not yet commented on the matter.

Skip next section Air alert sirens sound in Bahrain, Kuwait intercepts Iranian drones

Air alert sirens sound in Bahrain, Kuwait intercepts Iranian drones

Sirens warning of potential aerial threats sounded in Bahrain early on Wednesday amid the latest escalation between the US and Iran. 

Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said in a post on X: "A danger is present. The Ministry of Interior calls upon citizens and residents to adhere to calm, head to the nearest safe place, and follow the news through official channels, to safeguard public safety.

Bahrain is home to a major US naval base where the 5th Fleet is headquartered and has previously been targeted by Tehran.

Kuwait, another US ally in the Mideast region, also said it repelled attacks by "hostile" Iranian drones.

Skip next section US military says it completed strikes on targets in Iran

US military says it completed strikes on targets in Iran

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said that its latest wave of strikes against Iranian military targets has been completed.

"U.S. forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites," CENTCOM said in a statement.

It went on to say that the strikes came after "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members."

CENTCOM said there were currently 50,000 US military personnel operating in the Middle East.

Skip next section Jordan's military says Iranian missiles intercepted

Jordan's military says Iranian missiles intercepted

The Jordanian Armed Forces said that 10 ballistic missiles launched from Iran had been intercepted, while another three landed in remote areas.

"Jordan's air defence systems engaged 13 ballistic missiles that entered the Kingdom's airspace, successfully intercepting and destroying 10 of them, while three missiles fell in remote areas away from populated centres," a Jordanian military statement stated. Jordan added that no casualties had been reported.

Earlier, US President Donald Trump said that the latest strikes on Iran had been in response to Iranian missile launches at US targets on Monday and attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

Skip next section G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran

G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran.

"We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina.

"We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support."

He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with Iran's Revolutionary Guards.

"We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime."

Skip next section US launches strikes on Iran, Tehran fires back

US launches strikes on Iran, Tehran fires back

The United States has launched fresh strikes on targets in Iran as hostilities once again flare up. 

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."

"The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait," US President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social platform.

"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump warned.

Earlier, Trump told US broadcaster Fox News that US forces had struck Iranian radars.

“They tried to rebuild their radar because they can’t see anything,” Trump told Fox. “We waited until it was almost built and then we hit it."

An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, located around 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The US military announced it has launched new strikes on targets in Iran. Iran has vowed retaliation. 

The Iran war has been fought intermittently for the past 6 months and with the latest round of hostilities, there doesn't appear to be an end in sight to the conflict that is having major global economic repercussions.

Stay with us for updates and analysis on unfolding events in both Iran and the wider Middle East region.

entries.title: Ukraine: Russia threatens 'devastating' Baltic response
entries.summary: Any escalation in the Baltic region will lead to a significant response, Moscow said.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Russia threatens 'devastating' Baltic response

Published September 1, 2026last updated September 2, 2026

Any escalation in the Baltic region will lead to a significant response, Moscow said.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading!

Follow this blog for the latest news on Russia's war in Ukraine on September 1, 2026.

  • Russian strikes Kyiv, Odesa on first day of school year, killing at least 12
  • EU ministers focus on Ukraine air defenses, military support at Ireland talks
  • Drones trigger brief NATO response at Estonia's border with Russia

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section 'Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,' Zelenskyy warns

'Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,' Zelenskyy warns

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines flying across Russia, saying that Ukraine's drone operations would make the airspace unsafe.

"Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe," Zelenskyy said in a statement on Tuesday evening. He said that Ukraine was not threatening civilian aviation or individual aircraft.

"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said.

Just last week, Zelenskyy threatened the deployment of up to 1,000 long-range drones per day.

Russian President Vladimir Putin branded Zelenskyy's comments "a declaration of state terrorism."

"They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists," Putin said in a televised news conference.

Ukraine has been defending itself against a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022 and has repeatedly managed to strike targets deep inside Russia with drones as part of its defense efforts.

Skip next section Vessels hit near Odesa: Russia Defense Ministry

Vessels hit near Odesa: Russia Defense Ministry

Russia's military struck two cargo ships carrying military goods, the country's Defense Ministry said.

The vessels were hit in the port of Pivdennyi, ​near ​the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa, ​and ‌in the Black ​Sea.

Skip next section Russia, Ukraine hit each other's energy infrastructure

Russia, Ukraine hit each other's energy infrastructure

A Russian strike caused damage to a thermal power plant in the region of Odesa, southern Ukraine, state energy company Naftogaz said.

Elsewhere, Ukraine's military intelligence said that a strike by the Ukrainian army hit Russia's Novatek oil complex in the region of Leningrad.

Kyiv and Moscow have been exchanging blows in the past 24 hours, with energy infrastructure being targeted as part of the mutual strikes.

Skip next section Russia threatens 'devastating' response amid Baltic tensions

Russia threatens 'devastating' response amid Baltic tensions

Russia says it will "deliver a devastating response" to any hostile action against it in the Baltic region.

"In the event of a further escalation of the military-political situation in the Baltic region, it must be emphasized once again: Russia's response to the instigators of reckless anti-Russian ventures will be decisive. And they need to know this - it will be devastating for them," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at her weekly briefing.

It's not exactly clear what she was referring to, but earlier in the day a fire broke out at Russia's Baltic port of Ust-Luga following a drone attack according to the regional governor.

Separately, NATO scrambled military aircraft due to a possible air threat in Latvia's airspace near the town of Ludza, close to the Russian border.

Skip next section Russia sees no peace gains from Black Sea attack moratorium

Russia sees no peace gains from Black Sea attack moratorium

Russia does not believe a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea, a key grain shipping route, would bring a peaceful resolution to the war closer, Interfax quoted Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko as saying Tuesday.

Both sides have stepped up attacks in the Black Sea in recent months, driving global grain prices higher.

In mid-August, Ukraine reportedly conveyed an offer to Russia through a third party proposing that both sides halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea.

Monday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said his country had prepared a plan to ensure the safe passage of grain through the Black Sea and was working on an agreement similar to the 2022 grain deal that would facilitate safe exports.

Skip next section EU's Kallas says more interceptors needed to shield Ukrainian cities

EU's Kallas says more interceptors needed to shield Ukrainian cities

On Tuesday, European Union defense ministers discussed Ukraine's shortage of interceptor missiles needed to protect cities and civilians.

"July and August have been the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine," the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said on Tuesday about the deadly wave of strikes on Ukraine.

"Russia is really escalating, to hurt the people of Ukraine as much as possible, to break them," she said on the sidelines of a gathering of EU defense ministers in Wicklow in Ireland.

Against that backdrop, she said securing additional interceptors remains difficult because some countries face security pressures closer to home.

"We know that some of the countries have interceptors that will expire soon. So it would be very good if those would be given to Ukraine," Kallas said.

Beyond efforts to bolster air defenses, the EU is also working to unlock additional financial support for Ukraine's armed forces in the coming days.

Skip next section Germany says response to drone find near Ukrainian plane will be measured

Germany says response to drone find near Ukrainian plane will be measured

Germany's foreign minister said Berlin would respond in a measured way to the discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August. 

Johann Wadephul said the government was coordinating its approach with NATO and European Union partners.

The case sparked widespread speculation that Russia was responsible, though Berlin has not publicly assigned blame.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pledged a clear-cut response.

Despite declining to publicly assign responsibility, Wadephul stressed Germany would not be deterred by the incident.

"Germany will not be intimidated in any way, and that will continue to be the fundamental stance of our policy," Wadephul said, adding that Berlin "stands side by side with our Ukrainian partner."

"Russia must know that Germany is a stabilizing force in Europe, one that is always prepared to negotiate, but which will not be intimidated in any way."

Skip next section Ukraine says Russian missile and drone assault hits Kyiv, Odesa

Ukraine says Russian missile and drone assault hits Kyiv, Odesa

Ukraine's air force said Russia struck at least 28 locations in overnight attacks that continued into Tuesday, with debris falling at several additional sites.

The attack targeted Kyiv and the Odesa region and involved ballistic, cruise and anti-radar missiles, along with more than 200 drones and decoys.

At least 11 people were killed in the capital region:

  • Seven people were killed in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district; three others were wounded, including a child.
  • One Indian citizen was reported among those killed
  • One person was killed in the Holosiivskyi district after a building was hit and caught fire.
  • Three people were killed and 12 were injured elsewhere in the Kyiv region.

In Odesa, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian strike "deliberately damaged a border crossing point on the border with Romania, as well as export infrastructure."

Skip next section Ukraine reports August strikes on 54 Russian 'Shadow Fleet' ships

Ukraine reports August strikes on 54 Russian 'Shadow Fleet' ships

Russia and Ukraine are not only battling for dominance in the air with drones, but are also increasingly taking the drone war to the seas.

The commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brov, said Tuesday that his force struck 54 Russian "shadow fleet" vessels in August.

He did not immediately provide additional details.

Separately, Russia's state news agency Tass reported that Russia attacked "more than 150 seagoing vessels involved in military cargo deliveries for the Ukrainian army, as well as accompanying patrol boats, during the summer."

At least 70 of those attacks were recorded in August.

Skip next section EU defense ministers meet in Ireland to discuss Ukraine air defenses

EU defense ministers meet in Ireland to discuss Ukraine air defenses

European Union defense ministers are gathering in Wicklow, south of Dublin, for talks that are expected to focus on bolstering Ukraine's air defenses.

Moscow has taken advantage of Ukraine's shortage of US-built air defense missiles to pummel the country, while Kyiv has hit back against Russian infrastructure with its own long-range drone strikes.

There is also concern over Russia's apparent move to ramp up operations in Europe.

The ministers are also expected to discuss the bloc's support for Ukraine, including the implementation of a €90 billion ($104 billion) loan for Kyiv.

The loan, approved in April, aims to assist Kyiv with its most urgent economic and military needs as it continues to fight against Russia's full-scale invasion.

The talks are also expected cover further military assistance and closer cooperation between Ukraine's and the EU's defense industries.

Ministers are also expected to discuss the growing role of space in modern defense strategy.

EU foreign ministers are due to arrive later on Tuesday ahead of separate talks on Wednesday focused on continued support for Ukraine.

Skip next section NATO jets scrambled after drones briefly enter Estonian airspace

NATO jets scrambled after drones briefly enter Estonian airspace

NATO military aircraft were scrambled overnight after drones flew close to Estonia's border and briefly entered Estonian airspace, the country's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

The aircraft were launched from Amari Air Base, Tsahkna wrote in a post on social media.

"NATO reacted swiftly and exactly as planned. The Alliance is vigilant and ready to protect Allied territory," he added.

It was not immediately clear who launched the drones.

The incident highlights ongoing security concerns along NATO's eastern flank and is seen as a consequence of Russia's continuing war against Ukraine.

Skip next section Russian strike on Kyiv railway depot kills 7

Russian strike on Kyiv railway depot kills 7

Russia targeted Ukraine's capital for a sixth day in a row, including a ballistic missile strike on a railway depot in Kyiv that killed seven people.

"The ballistic strike took the lives of 7 people, 6 of whom were our employees. 1 colleague is in hospital with injuries," Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, chief executive of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine's state-owned railway network said, adding that "there is extensive destruction."

Emergency services said eight people were killed and five wounded in Kyiv, including three children, as fires broke out across several parts of the capital during the overnight attacks.

Elsewhere in the Kyiv region, one person was killed and nine others, including a child, were injured after missiles and drones struck an apartment building and a business facility in Boryspil.

The attacks marked the sixth consecutive day of Russian strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region.

Russia's Defense Ministry said it targeted military and energy facilities in Kyiv, Odesa, and nearby areas.

Across the border in Russia's Belgorod region, one person was killed in a Ukrainian attack, acting Governor Alexander Shuvayev said.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

European defense ministers are meeting in Ireland today and are expected to hear from Ukraine's new acting defense minister, Yevgeniy Khmara.

He is likely to point to the latest wave of Russian attacks, now entering a sixth straight day, as Moscow continues its campaign against Kyiv and surrounding areas.

Ukrainian officials have repeatedly argued that the sustained bombardment underscores the urgent need for additional air defense systems.

The meeting comes as several European countries are also strengthening their own military capabilities, partly in response to a growing number of drone-related incidents near their borders.

Overnight, Estonia reported a new drone incursion into its airspace, adding to concerns about regional security.

We'll be following these developments, along with other key events in Russia's war against Ukraine, throughout the day in this blog.
